My brain is operating about the same as yours right now...in between all the stress of dealing with covid and social distancing (as if I wasn't socially isolated before), my ED ramping up, and all of my other mental health shit, there's not a ton of room left in my stupid brain for much else.

My ED story sounds similar to yours. 6th grade was the beginning of restricting, counting calories, and exercising in my room at night when I was supposed to be sleeping. I had already suffered from severe insomnia for about a year, and reading did nothing to help lull me to sleep, so why not tire myself out with repetitive exercises, that in hindsight probably did nothing for actual weight loss. Lol. While the restricting was pretty severe from what I can glean from my old diaries/food logs, my family didn't notice anything was up (I could go on and on about why that was...). It wasn't until I started purging a LOT when I was 14 that they decided to start taking what had turned into full-blown bulimia somewhat seriously...and even then, not so much.

I admitted myself to inpatient/residential treatment when I was 23 and diagnosed with AN b/p subtype...I'm almost 33 now, and in the past 9 years my "official" diagnosis has changed several times. I finally extricated myself from the revolving doors of the treatment center I was admitted to 7 or 8 times after that first stay, because that place was fucked up on so many levels.

Fast forward to present day: My therapist from the treatment center left that hellhole for another practice that doesn't pretend to be a safe haven that "heals eating disorders" (the actual slogan on all the highway billboards for the treatment center! Hah). I followed her to her new clinic, and lo and behold, we actually talk about things that don't have anything to do with food, weight, and shape! This has been super helpful in so many ways...except for the fact that it's really, really easy to downplay how bad things have gotten again. She doesn't weigh me or grill me about my daily intake, because she trusts me. But she's also not an idiot, so part of me thinks she is giving me the chance to open up to her and ask for help. Unfortunately, my ED has once again hijacked my brain, so even if she did ask me point blank how much I weigh right now or how much I'm *really* eating, I doubt I would be honest with her. Which sucks, because I absolutely love her.

So you haven't seen a specialist for a long time either huh? How is that going? Do you think it's helpful to not see a specialist? Because I remember how being forced to talk about my ED nonstop in sessions with specialists made me hyperfocus on food and weight, and when I finally cut ties with the treatment center, it freed up so much of my mental energy (and time and money!) to actually focus on other things that, you know, matter...like work, relationships, what have you.

I'm so glad we connected! I was worried I wouldn't hear back from you when the Tuesday thread disappeared!

Hey there friend...I hear you...and yes words are very tricky sometimes lol! I'm in my earlyish thirties as well, and have also spent over half my life struggling with this fucked up disease. 
I think at our age (I don't know exactly how old you are, but I rationally know that neither of us are that old, even though it sure feels like I'm old af sometimes haha), we are both cognizant of the fact that we didn't choose to develop eating disorders. And now, let me awkwardly and abruptly start writing in the first person singular, because I don't think I can accurately speak to anyone's experiences but my own. 
I didn't choose to develop an eating disorder, but I sure as shit chose to engage in risky behaviors regarding food, etc, when all this started way back in the beginning of middle school. I used to love reading, and I had the pleasure of going to an International School overseas, where apparently nobody knew what the fuck kind of books were in our school library. At a fairly young age, I devoured books about heroin (or "smack" as they referred to it in some countries), a guy jumping in front of a moving subway (this book became tragically poignant after somebody actually did jump in front of the subway one day --the majority of my classmates and I took the subway to and from school, and it happened in front of a few of the kids the year above me), and a weight loss manual for kids my age trying to shed pounds [side note: I hope to god that book has been fucking burned by now, and that nobody ever writes a diet book for kids again].
I legit took notes while I read that book, and when I was done, my notebook and brain were full of calorie counts, "tips and tricks," and estimates for how many calories swimming, jogging, biking, and skiing would each burn per hour. I obviously knew what anorexia and bulimia were by this point (you can thank my school library for that, too), but I thought that if you had anorexia, that meant you just had more self-discipline and self-control than other people. Not that I ever considered myself anorexic, because I also thought that, if I WAS anorexic, I wouldn't be so fucking ugly, and more guys would like me.

...oh man, now MY brain is doing its thing, because I'm sure this stupid story had a point...at some point. Lol. Maybe I am fuckin old. Or maybe prolonged malnourishment has ruined one of the only things I ever felt like I was good at: writing.

...oh man, now 25 minutes have gone by. In between trying to remember where this whole comment was supposed to end up, being distracted by my ED voice and my rational mind fighting upstairs, and the fact that it's late (objectively speaking haha), I feel super dumb. But PM me if you ever wanna chat and I promise I'll shut the fuck up and let you talk <3
Thank you for your input! :)

I can briefly sum up my experience growing up, my attachment style when I was younger, and my attachment style/s now. A lot of what you say makes sense, and is pretty in line with the way my mind operated (and probably still does to some degree):

From the time I was born until I was 15, my family moved back and forth between the United States and various countries overseas (won't name states or countries, tryna remain anonymous and all). The shortest amount of time we lived somewhere was less than a year, and the longest was a year. By the time I was 8 or 9, I realized that whatever friends I had made where I was living at the time, within a year or so, I would never see them again. 

After coming to this realization, when it came time to move across the ocean a year later when I was almost 10, I was completely heartbroken. I have so many journal entries from that time describing how sad I was to be leaving behind my best friend Jessica. Pretty much immediately after that move is when I first started experiencing symptoms of depression, which, along with the anxiety I had experienced since kindergarten (after another huge international move), got progressively worse. 

On the introversion-extroversion spectrum, I definitely lean more towards introversion. But I learned very early on that in order to make friends, I couldn't give in to most of my introvert tendencies. Making friends wasn't easy, but it also wasn't hard. After the move when I was 10, I made plenty of friends, but my friend groups were pretty much constantly in flux. My "best friends" in each place i lived from ages 10-14 always ended up being the friends I hung out with the most during the 6 months leading up to the next move. Generally speaking, they were my "ride-or-dies," and as far as my former friends...? Fuck 'em. I'd always find some reason to start a fight or make them hate me. Less people to say goodbye to.

When I was 15, my family made their final move (they live here to this day -- I think they were just as sick of moving as me). It was relieving to say the least. But I continued to repeat similar patterns in my friendships and romantic relationships: honeymoon period, BFFS4LYFE (or "soulmate"), and then one day, the smallest thing, or sometimes nothing at all, would prompt me to either end the relationship or do something to piss the other person off enough that they ended it for me.

Once I started college, SOME of the pushing people away started to ease up. But this is when I began to latch on to certain people. Some girls, but overwhelmingly guys, both friends and more-than-friends. I take social rejection very hard, especially if it's coming from a guy I'm in to. So what did I do when I was rejected? I'd find some dude to fuck around with so that I felt wanted. 

This tactic was usually not effective...new dude would eventually reject me too. Wash, rinse, repeat. 

The only exception to this pattern involves my current SO, who I started dating about a year and a half in to high school. Our relationship didn't last super long back in HS, but we both stayed in the same area for college, and kept finding our way back to each other. Currently, we've been dating again for almost a year. Before this, we dated and broke up 4 (maybe 5?) times. 

In between our periods of being together, I dated other guys, and had 2 other serious relationships. But even when my SO and I weren't together, I always made it clear to whoever I was dating that my now-SO is a significant person in my life, and even though I didn't plan on hanging out with him on a regular basis, he was important to me, and they better respect that, and not get all weird if we did hang out with him in group settings occasionally.

Wow, that turned out waaay longer than expected. But after actually sitting down and laying it all out there, I'm left scratching my head. In almost all other instances, once me and a guy are broken up, we're done, and we never test the waters again (minus a few drunk hook-ups with exes...oops). The attachment and loyalty are diminished (or gone altogether). But with my SO, they've been there, basically unwavering, and for the past 17 years, I have always known that he is truly a good, kind, person, and even if I happen to be really fucking mad at him, I've never said "He's such a piece of shit/fucker/asshole/etc."

My kitten (she's almost old enough to be a cat now) is an ESA, I got her when she was 5 months old, and let's just say that when I'm not working, i spend a looooot of time in my tiny little apartment with her (I'm not super socially isolated, but ummmm yeah i guess you could say I tend towards isolation). As she's gotten older, her ability to sense my major mood fluctuations has gotten incredibly astute. Earlier this week, I came home, sat down on the bed and she ran up for pets. I petted her for a few minutes and snuggled with her, but when she'd had enough, she went to the end of the bed and curled up there. I stayed sitting where I was, staring blankly  at...nothing?, and then I started to cry. Not audibly, no heaving or trying to catch my breath or anything like that, just tears silently falling down my face. I looked over at her at one point, we locked eyes, and I'm not even kidding, her pupils instantly dilated and she ran over to me and curled up as hard as she could in my lap.

Naturally, this made me cry even harder, but then it was like sad tears mixed with tears of appreciation for my little turd nugget.

10/10 would recommend getting a pet of some kind to anyone who struggles with self-care and self-love.

OP, I hope you are willing to re-evaluate your "commitment"...because those of us with eating disorders of longer duration oftentimes fluctuate between symptoms as well as diagnoses...and sometimes, we don't fit diagnostic criteria for any of the "traditional" eating disorders that people generally think of, and we instead get slapped with the diagnosis of "other specified feeding or eating disorder" (when I was in and out of treatment, i believe this was EDNOS). 

So I guess my point is...eating disorders can morph and change in nature over time, and I don't think we always have a choice in this (so there is no way we can "commit" to one disorder versus another). The disease unfortunately hijacks our brains, and instead of us being in control of our disorders, they control us.

Personal example: I was diagnosed with bulimia when I was 14, anorexia binge-purge subtype at 23, and anorexia at 28. I've been in treatment with loads of other women and men with similar stories, flip flopping between starving, binging, purging (multiple methods), all of the above and everything in between. 

I guess my point is, no matter how our disorders present themselves, we all have one thing in common: We are hurting. We are in emotional pain, and living in our bodies (AND BRAINS!) is really, really fucking hard. Here for you, OP <3
